narrative_idea_gen: A combat medic's weekly poker circle on a remote forward operating base in Helmand Province keeps losing players—not to bad hands but to IEDs and sniper fire—while the group's ringleader, a deeply indebted, Percocet-dependent sergeant named Dorsey, refuses to fold the game, raising the stakes with morbid theatricality each time a chair empties. The story cuts between two timelines: one where Dorsey got clean after a catastrophic gambling debt triggered a breakdown and spent his final months trying to keep his remaining guys alive through grim, sober discipline, and another where he spiraled deeper into oxy and all-night hands, becoming funnier and more magnetically reckless as the body count climbed—and only one of these versions actually happened. Their base chaplain narrates both realities with the exhausted omniscience of a man who has heard every private confession on the FOB, who knows what Dorsey's wife wrote in the letters he burned unread, who understands exactly which version Dorsey needed to be true and which version God, or nobody, allowed. The dark comedy bleeds from the squad's elaborate coping rituals—renaming poker hands after killed friends, running a deadpool board disguised as a March Madness bracket, Dorsey's rule that anyone who folds before the river owes the dead guy's family fifty bucks—while the chaplain's narration slowly, mercilessly collapses the two timelines into one, revealing that the version where Dorsey tried was always the fantasy, and the only real winner at the table was the war itself.

narrative_beats:
# Seven Structural Beats for *The Last Hand* (working title)

---

## Beat 1: The Chaplain's Confessional Frame

**What Happens:** The chaplain introduces himself—not by name but by function. He is the man people talk to when they can't talk to anyone else. He establishes, in a voice of practiced, weary precision, that he is going to tell the story of Sergeant Dorsey and the poker game, but that there are two versions, and he heard them both, and he is no longer certain which one Dorsey told him and which one he constructed afterward from the wreckage of what Dorsey told him. He does not yet say which version is real. He may say something like: *I'll tell you both, and you can do what I couldn't, which is choose.*

**Structural Function — Frame Narration as Compromised Sacrament:** This is your classical-Chinese preface. The chaplain is the institutional voice—the military's designated listener, the man whose job is to hold confession without the Catholic infrastructure, to provide "spiritual fitness" in a system that can't afford spiritual complexity. His authority is real (he *did* hear every confession on the FOB) and fraudulent (hearing confessions didn't give him the power to save anyone). The frame must establish that the narrator knows more than any character in the story, including Dorsey, while simultaneously establishing that this surplus of knowledge has purchased him nothing. He is omniscient and impotent. That combination—total information, zero agency—is the chaplain's specific wound, and it is what qualifies him to narrate and disqualifies him from resolving anything.

**Why It Must Work This Way:** The dual-timeline structure will collapse later, but it must be *installed* here with an honest announcement that it exists. Lu Xun buried his conclusion in his preface; you need to bury yours. The chaplain's opening admission—*I don't know which version is real*—sounds like humble candor. By the end, the reader will understand it was a lie of omission: the chaplain has always known. He is not confused; he is *grieving the version that didn't happen*, and his narration is the last place where that version gets to live. The frame is not a neutral container. It is the chaplain's own coping ritual, formally identical to Dorsey's poker game: a structure you maintain because the alternative is admitting what you already know.

**The Tonal Key:** The chaplain's voice should sound like exhaustion that has aged into a kind of precision. Not literary—administrative. The way a man talks when he has written too many condolence-adjacent emails and learned that the cleaner the sentence, the less likely he is to start crying in the middle of it. The warmth should be detectable but buried, like heat under sand.

---

## Beat 2: The Full Table

**What Happens:** The poker game at its height. Every chair filled. The chaplain describes the players—not as characters in a war story but as poker players, with their tells, their habits, their buy-in superstitions. Dorsey runs the game with manic precision: fixed schedule, house rules hand-laminated in plastic sleeves, a buy-in jar made from a Pringles can. The FOB exists around them—mortar alarms, generator hum, the obscene heat—but the table is presented as a pocket of liturgical order. Dorsey is introduced in both timelines simultaneously, and at this early stage, they are nearly identical: he's funny, he's indebted, he palms Percocets like peanuts, he's the kind of NCO who holds a unit together through sheer force of personality. The two Dorseys haven't diverged yet. The reader shouldn't even feel the split.

**Structural Function — Establishing the Ritual Before Defiling It:** You need a scene of fullness so the subsequent emptying has material to work against. Every named player at this table is structural inventory: each one is a chair that will later be empty, a poker hand that will later be renamed, a line item on the deadpool bracket. The reader must be allowed to experience the game as the players experience it—as a *good thing*, a genuine refuge, a functioning ritual. If you start with irony, the dark comedy has nothing to darken from. The table must feel briefly sacred so that its systematic desecration registers.

**Why It Must Work This Way:** The two timelines must begin fused. This is critical. If you introduce them as separate tracks from the start, the reader will treat them as a puzzle to solve—*which one is real?*—and will read analytically rather than emotionally. By starting in a zone where both Dorseys are the same Dorsey, you bond the reader to a single figure. The divergence, when it comes, should feel like something *happening to a person the reader knows*, not like a structural conceit being demonstrated. Additionally, Dorsey's table-running behavior—the laminated rules, the Pringles can, the performative authority—needs to be established as character before it becomes pathology. The rituals are endearing here. They will be horrifying by Beat 6.

**The Tonal Key:** This should be the funniest section of the story. Let the squad banter work. Let the chaplain's narration be wryly affectionate, almost nostalgic, before he remembers what he's narrating toward. The comedy is genuine—these men are actually funny, the way people in extremity are funny—and the chaplain loved them. That love is what makes his narration a confession rather than a report.

---

## Beat 3: The First Empty Chair

**What Happens:** A player dies. The chaplain names the cause with flat specificity (IED, route name, vehicle position, time of day). The next poker night, the chair is empty. *This* is where the timelines diverge. In Timeline A (the sober version), Dorsey looks at the chair, says nothing for a long time, then quietly pockets his Percocet stash and dumps it (or hands it to the medic, or some equivalent gesture of renunciation). In Timeline B (the spiral version), Dorsey looks at the chair, says something lethally funny—some remark so dark the whole table laughs despite themselves—and raises the stakes. He takes twice his usual dose. He's *more* alive. The chaplain narrates both, switching between them with a connective as casual as a paragraph break, or a simple "Or:" or "In the other version:"

**Structural Function — The Fork, and the Introduction of the Reader's Desire:** This is where the story's real engine ignites: the reader's *preference*. By presenting both timelines as equally plausible and giving each a distinct emotional logic—A is the one where Dorsey fights, B is the one where Dorsey burns—you force the reader to invest in A. Not because A is more convincing, but because the reader *wants* A to be real. This desire is the story's deepest subject. The chaplain wants it too. The structure is designed to exploit that want and ultimately to indict it—not cruelly, but with the merciless compassion of someone who held the same hope and watched it fail.

**Why It Must Work This Way:** The first death cannot be random; it must produce a *choice*. Dorsey's response to the first empty chair is the hinge of his character. In A, loss produces discipline. In B, loss produces performance. Both are recognizable human responses. Both are, in their way, forms of refusal—refusal to be defeated by the loss, refusal to let the game end. The structural trick is that B is actually the timeline where Dorsey is *more compelling as a character*—funnier, wilder, more magnetically watchable—while A is the timeline where he is *more admirable as a person*. The reader wants A to be true but is drawn to B. This asymmetry is the knife. It should hurt more and more as the story progresses, because the version that's better to watch is the version that kills him.

**The Tonal Key:** The death itself should be reported in the chaplain's administrative voice—clipped, procedural, almost bureaucratic. A date, a grid reference, a euphemism ("sustained injuries inconsistent with continued life" or some ghastly equivalent the chaplain has learned from official channels). Then the poker scene: warm, human, painfully specific. The contrast between the institutional language of death and the intimate language of coping is the chaplain's whole existence, compressed into a transition.

---

## Beat 4: The Rituals of the Table

**What Happens:** The dark-comedy machinery is deployed in full. The squad begins renaming poker hands after dead players—a pair of sevens becomes "Bakers" because Baker always played sevens, a flush becomes a "Cortez" for reasons that are funny only if you knew Cortez. The deadpool board goes up, disguised as a March Madness bracket (necessary deniability if brass visits). Dorsey institutes the fifty-dollar rule: fold before the river, you owe the most recently killed player's family fifty bucks. The rule is enforced. Money is actually sent. In Timeline A, these rituals take on a sober, almost religious quality—Dorsey policing them with the grim care of a man maintaining a memorial. In Timeline B, they're wilder, meaner, funnier—Dorsey turning grief into a floor show, the rituals escalating because escalation is the only direction left.

**Structural Function — The Coping Mechanism as Central Metaphor, and the Story's Dark-Comedy Credentials:** This beat is where the story earns its genre. The rituals are simultaneously (a) genuinely funny, (b) genuinely functional—these men are processing death the only way available to them, (c) genuinely disturbing if you step outside the FOB's moral atmosphere, and (d) the structural equivalent of the madman's diary entries: a system of meaning-making that might be sane or insane depending on where you're standing. The fifty-dollar rule is the single best invention in the premise. It transforms the poker game from metaphor into *mechanism*: the game now has a real-world ethical consequence, because folding—quitting, giving up, refusing to play—costs you money that goes to the dead. Staying in the hand = honoring the dead. The game becomes a debt structure, exactly mirroring Dorsey's actual gambling debt and his Percocet debt to his own body.

**Why It Must Work This Way:** The rituals must accumulate. Each dead player adds a named hand, a bracket entry, a new invocation. The table becomes a palimpsest of the dead, the way the history book in Lu Xun becomes a palimpsest of cannibalism. The reader should begin to feel the weight: each funny new name is a body. The comedy does not relieve the horror; it *is* the horror, metabolized into a form the living can swallow. The chaplain's narration should register this without editorializing—he understands what the rituals are because ritual is his professional domain. He knows a liturgy when he sees one, even when it's built from poker chips and dead-man jokes. His restraint in not calling it sacred is itself a form of respect.

**The Tonal Key:** Maximum gallows humor. Let the reader laugh. The laughter is the point. The laughter is what makes the abyss visible, because you can feel the abyss in the exact half-second after you laugh—that catch, that beat of silence, where you know what you just laughed at. Dorsey's gift, in both timelines, is that he can keep people in the laughing part. The chaplain's curse is that he lives in the half-second after.

---

## Beat 5: The Burned Letters and What the Chaplain Knows

**What Happens:** The chaplain reveals, in a passage that feels almost involuntary—as though the narration is confessing something the narrator didn't plan to share—that he knows what Dorsey's wife wrote in the letters Dorsey burned unread. He knows because she sent copies to him. Or because she called the chaplain line. Or because Dorsey, in one of their sessions, described the letters perfectly while claiming he'd never opened them. The content: she's leaving, she's not leaving, the debt collectors are calling, their daughter asked where he is, she can't do this, she'll wait, she won't wait. The chaplain reveals this not as exposition but as the moment his two timelines become hardest to hold apart, because the letters are *the same in both versions*. Dorsey's wife doesn't know which Dorsey she's married to. She's responding to an absence that is the same shape in both realities.

**Structural Function — The Anchor of Unnarrated Reality, and the Chaplain's Private Guilt:** This is the beat that breaks the dual-timeline conceit out of its neatly managed architecture and introduces something neither timeline can contain: the world outside the FOB, the family that exists regardless of which version of Dorsey is real. The burned letters are the story's equivalent of Lu Xun's "reading between the lines"—they are the text-within-the-text that, once revealed, reframes everything. Dorsey burning them *unread* is the crucial detail. In Timeline A (sober), it could mean he's protecting himself from emotional chaos so he can focus on keeping his guys alive. In Timeline B (spiral), it could mean he can't face what he's become. Both interpretations are plausible. Neither is comfortable. The chaplain's knowledge of their contents—when Dorsey didn't know them, or pretended not to—makes the chaplain complicit in a way he has not previously acknowledged. He held information that might have changed things. He didn't use it. This is his confession within the confession.

**Why It Must Work This Way:** The letters prevent the story from becoming hermetically sealed inside its own set-piece cleverness. The poker game, the rituals, the dual timelines—these could become a self-admiring machine if you let them. The letters are the human mess that the machine can't process. A woman writing to a man who won't read her words. A daughter's question. The debt, which is not a metaphor—it is an actual number, owed to actual creditors, threatening an actual family. This beat grounds the allegory in the domestic, just as Lu Xun grounds his allegory in the dead sister. And like the dead sister, the wife and daughter exist in a zone of damage that the narrator's structural games cannot aesthetic
narrative_story:
# The Last Hand

## I.

I am not going to tell you my name because my name was never the point. I was the chaplain. I say this the way you'd say I was the plumber or I was the one with the clipboard—a function, not a person, and if you've ever been on a forward operating base you know the difference matters. My job was to be available. A twenty-four-hour service line with a divinity degree and a government-issue Bible I kept next to a copy of the Bhagavad Gita and a Quran with a cracked spine, because you cover your bases or you don't, and either way someone's going to bleed out calling for a God you haven't read up on.

I heard everything. That was the duty. People talked to me because I was the last option before silence, and silence on a FOB is the thing that kills you—not the mortars, not the heat, not the route clearance at 0430 with your balls in your throat. The silence. The part where you lie on your rack and the plywood ceiling is eleven inches from your face and you realize that no one in your life back home can hear what you're actually saying, and you have been screaming in a frequency only dogs and chaplains can detect.

So they came to me, and I listened, and I wrote nothing down, and I told no one, and I carried it. That was the architecture of the thing. I was a load-bearing wall in a building that was always on fire.

The story I'm going to tell you is about Sergeant First Class David Dorsey and a poker game that ran every Thursday night for seven months on FOB Copperhead, Paktika Province, 2009. I heard the story from Dorsey himself, across six sessions in my office—which was half a shipping container with a rug I'd bought at the bazaar in Sharana and a sign on the door that said CHAPLAIN in letters I'd stenciled with a Sharpie because the official placard never arrived.

There are two versions.

I used to know which one he told me and which one I built later, at night, on a cot, in the dark, revising his confession the way you revise a letter you'll never send—changing a word here, a gesture there, until the man in the story does the thing you needed him to do instead of the thing he did. I used to know. It has been fifteen years, and the seam where his version ends and mine begins has been walked over so many times that I can no longer feel the ridge under my feet.

I could lie to you. I could tell you the clean version, the one I rehearsed for the after-action review I was never asked to give. Or I could tell you the one that wakes me up. But I have been in the business of listening long enough to know that choosing for somebody else is the most violent thing you can do while sitting still.

So I'll tell you both. And you can do what I couldn't, which is choose.

---

## II.

Thursdays at 2100, the game.

Dorsey ran it out of the MWR tent, which was a generous name for a plywood box with a television that received four channels, three of which were AFN and one of which was, through some satellite miracle no one could explain, a Turkish cooking show. The television was always on. Nobody watched it. It was atmosphere. Dorsey said a card room needed background noise or it was just a bunch of men staring at each other, and that was called group therapy, and group therapy was my department, not his.

He called meetings of more than three people without cards a "vulnerability." He said this with a straight face.

The table was a sheet of plywood on sawhorses, covered with a green felt remnant that Dorsey had procured from God knows where—he said eBay, which meant someone's wife or mother had shipped it in a care package, which meant Dorsey had traded something for it, probably Rip Its or baby wipes or one of the favors he dispensed like a ward boss. The felt was stained with coffee rings and Tabasco and a brown mark in one corner that might have been blood and might have been dip spit and that Dorsey had circled with a silver Sharpie and labeled DEALER'S BLESSING, which was the kind of joke that only works at war, where everything is a little bit sacred because nothing is.

House rules. Dorsey had typed them. Single-spaced, twelve-point Times New Roman, printed on the operations center printer at 0300 when the battle captain wasn't looking, and then laminated—laminated—in the supply office, because Dorsey understood that lamination conferred authority. You do not argue with a laminated document. You obey it the way you obey a posted speed limit: not because you believe in it but because someone cared enough to make a sign.

Rule one: Texas Hold 'Em only. No Omaha, no stud, no "weird shit" (Dorsey's language, laminated).

Rule two: Buy-in is twenty dollars. Rebuy once. No credit.

Rule three: The buy-in goes in the can. The can was a Pringles tube, sour cream and onion, with the top cut off and HOUSE FUND written on the side in electrical tape. Where the fund went was never explained. People stopped asking.

Rule four: No rank at the table. "When you sit down, you're a player. I don't care if you're a private or you're Jesus Christ in multicam, you check your shit at the door." This was in the laminated rules. The word "shit" was laminated.

Rule five: The chaplain has a standing seat but is not required to bet. This was Dorsey's gift to me, or his way of keeping an eye on me, or both. I sat in most weeks. I folded a lot. I watched.

And the players. Let me tell you about the players, because you need to see the table full before you can feel it empty, and that is the whole point, if this story has a point, which I have spent fifteen years trying to decide.

Baker, the specialist, twenty-two, from Baton Rouge, who played every hand like it was his last—which was a metaphor he would not have appreciated and which, as it turned out, was not a metaphor. Baker bet with his jaw. When he had cards, his jaw relaxed. When he was bluffing, he chewed the inside of his cheek so hard you could see the muscle working through his skin. He didn't know he did this. Nobody told him.

Cortez, staff sergeant, thirty-one, on his fourth deployment, the kind of man who had been blown up so many times his body had a residual vibration, like a tuning fork that never stops ringing. Cortez played tight. Cortez played like a man who understood that the universe was a game of negative expected value and still sat down. He folded more than anyone. When he won, he didn't celebrate. He stacked his chips with the care of a man defusing a bomb, which he had literally done, twice, before he transferred to infantry because he said explosives were too predictable.

Little Nguyen—called that to distinguish him from Big Nguyen, who was in second platoon and never played poker because he said gambling was a sin, which I respected even though I thought he was wrong, not about gambling but about the taxonomy of sin, which in my experience is less a hierarchy and more a weather system. Little Nguyen was nineteen and played poker the way puppies play with shoes—no strategy, all enthusiasm, an endless willingness to be destroyed. He lost every week. He lost with joy. He once went all-in on a two-seven offsuit because, he said, "it felt right, Chap, it felt *right*," and when he was annihilated by Dorsey's full house, he laughed so hard he fell off his chair, which was a folding camp chair, which collapsed, which made everyone laugh, and for a moment—for one moment—the plywood box with the Turkish cooking show was the best room in the world.

Pettigrew, the medic, who shouldn't have been there because medics weren't assigned to the FOB's organic unit, but who had drifted in the way people drift in at war—he was covering for a medic who was covering for a medic who had been medevacked with shrapnel in his left kidney, and the covering kept extending until Pettigrew was just theirs, a borrowed man who became permanent through the alchemy of shared danger. Pettigrew played recklessly but knew the odds. He'd been pre-med before he enlisted. He had a calculator behind his eyes. He bet like a maniac because he was bored and because arithmetic, at a certain point, is its own kind of adrenaline.

Tomaszewski—Ski, always Ski—the platoon sergeant, who outranked Dorsey but deferred to him at the table because the table was Dorsey's country. Ski played one hand an hour. The rest of the time he sat with his arms folded and a dip in his lip and watched, running a parallel poker game in his head that he sometimes described aloud: "I would have bet there. I would have check-raised. You're dead." He was usually right. He never won because he never played, and this too was a metaphor he would not have appreciated.

And Dorsey.

Dorsey, who dealt with the speed of a man who'd worked card rooms before the Army, which he had—Atlantic City, two summers, dealing blackjack to tourists and learning that the house always wins because the house controls the architecture. Dorsey, who was thirty-four and looked forty-four and moved like a man held together by willpower and ibuprofen. Dorsey, whose Percocet habit was the worst-kept secret on the FOB—he palmed them openly, popped them mid-hand, chased them with Rip Its. He had a bad back, two bad knees, and a left shoulder that dislocated if he raised his arm above ninety degrees, which meant he threw grenades side-arm, like a pitcher with a torn rotator cuff, which terrified everyone in his squad because side-arm grenades are, aerodynamically speaking, a nightmare.

He was funny. I have to tell you he was funny because the rest of this will make no sense if you don't understand the specific quality of his humor, which was the kind that made you feel less alone in exact proportion to how dark the material was. He could say things about death that would have been monstrous from anyone else and from him were—I don't have the word. Not comforting. Not cathartic. *Accurate.* He was accurate about the horror, and accuracy, when you are surrounded by institutional euphemism, is a form of love.

He owed nineteen thousand dollars in gambling debt to various entities back home, a fact he shared with me in our first session and with the poker table in the second week, announcing it as though it were a credential: "You're playing with a professional loser, gentlemen. I have been losing at a level most of you will never achieve." Everyone laughed. The debt was real. The debt was destroying his marriage. But at the table—at the table—saying it out loud made it a chip in a game, a thing with known value, a problem that fit inside a structure. And a problem that fits inside a structure is a problem you can survive.

Both Dorseys did this. Both Dorseys ran the table, popped the pills, owed the money, made the jokes. Both Dorseys loved those men with the fierce, unspoken, operationally necessary love that the Army has no vocabulary for and that the chaplain's office is supposed to hold in trust.

At this point in the story, there is only one Dorsey.

You wouldn't feel the split.

---

## III.

Specialist Marcus Baker was killed on 14 March 2009 at approximately 1347 hours local time when the vehicle in which he was traveling, an M-ATV in the number-three position of a four-vehicle patrol, struck a pressure-plate improvised explosive device on Route Copper, vicinity grid 42S VD 1487 3902, Paktika Province, Afghanistan. Specialist Baker, who was seated in the right rear passenger position, sustained injuries inconsistent with continued life. He was pronounced dead at the scene by the patrol medic. He was twenty-two years old. His next of kin, a mother in Baton Rouge, was notified at 0215 Central time by a casualty notification team from Fort Polk, Louisiana. The team consisted of a captain and a chaplain. I know this because I was copied on the notification report, as I was copied on all notification reports, because that was procedure, and procedure was the rope you held in the dark even when you couldn't feel the texture.

Grid 42S VD 1487 3902. That's a piece of road about the width of a Walmart aisle. That's the amount of earth required to end a person. I have the grid memorized. I have all the grids memorized. They are the only prayers I say now that mean anything, because a grid coordinate is at least honest—it tells you where something happened, not why, and I have learned to prefer the where.

Thursday came.

The table was set. Dorsey had set it—he always set it, an hour early, aligning the chips, checking the felt for debris, slotting the Pringles can in its place on the folding table to the right of the dealer's position. Everything precise. Everything in order. Seven chairs arranged around the plywood, and one of them—Baker's chair, the chair on the south side—was empty.

This is where I lose the thread. This is where I need you to hold two things in your head at once and understand that I held them for fifteen years and that the weight has shifted over time, the way a load shifts in a rucksack on a long march, and what started on my shoulders now sits on my chest.

In one version:

Dorsey looked at the chair. He didn't sit immediately. The others had filed in—Cortez, Little Nguyen, Pettigrew, Ski, two others whose names I will not use because they asked me not to—and they stood or sat and they all looked at the chair and nobody spoke. The Turkish cooking show played on the television. A woman was julienning carrots. The generator hummed. Somewhere on the FOB a door slammed in the wind.

Dorsey stood behind his dealer's seat and looked at Baker's chair for a long time. Maybe thirty seconds. Maybe a minute. In a room full of soldiers, a minute of silence has the weight of an avalanche.

Then he reached into the cargo pocket of his pants—the right cargo pocket, the one where he kept the amber bottle—and he pulled out his Percocets. The bottle was almost full. He looked at it the way you look at a letter you've decided not to send. And he walked to Pettigrew, the medic, and he put the bottle in Pettigrew's hand and closed Pettigrew's fingers around it and said: "I'm done with these. If I ask for them back, tell me to go fuck myself."

Pettigrew looked at the bottle. Looked at Dorsey. Said: "Roger that."

And Dorsey sat down and shuffled the deck and said: "Blinds are up. Sit down or go home."

Or:

Dorsey looked at the chair. Same room, same men, same julienned carrots on the television, same thirty seconds or minute of silence that weighed the same in both versions because silence doesn't know it's being narrated two ways.

And Dorsey said: "Baker would've folded. Baker always folded. Man played poker like a nun at a strip club—technically present, spiritually horrified." A beat. "Pair of sevens. That was his hand. Every goddamn time, he'd chase a pair of sevens to the river like it owed him money." Another beat. "From now on, a pair of sevens is called Bakers."

Little Nguyen laughed first. It came out of him like a wound opening—not because it was funny but because the pressure had to go somewhere. Then Cortez laughed. Then everyone laughed, even Ski, who hadn't laughed in four months.

narrative_idea_gen_original_prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection

Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. A hallway mirror offers a glimpse of their anxious posture before they turn away. 1000 words.
